name: Aaron Benzrihem Ankle Pick System
description: Study gi ankle-pick connections with a focused Aaron Benzrihem course match, practical partner drills, clear decisions, and ways to review your progress.
summary: The Aaron Benzrihem Ankle Pick System links gi grips and off-balancing to same-side or cross-body ankle picks from standing, seated guard, and a three-point stance.
overview:
An ankle can be within reach without being a useful takedown target. Build the upper-body connection first, observe which foot the opponent makes available, and choose a finishing direction that matches the grip. Comparing standing and seated starts can help you see when the same idea needs a different entry.

Basics To Advanced: Ankle Picks For Jiu Jitsu by Aaron Benzrihem is the matched instructional. Benzrihem distinguishes standing, seated, and three-point starts, with same-side and cross-body finishes and setups from feints and grip changes. The drills, sequence, and assessment criteria below are an original BJJGraph study plan; use them to organize practice alongside the course and feedback from a coach.
key_principles: Choose the target ankle in relation to the upper-body grip.
Prompt a step before reaching down without support.
Keep standing and seated starting conditions distinct.
Maintain balance as the level changes.
Continue through the landing rather than stopping at ankle contact.

common_obstacles.obstacle: You touch the ankle but the opponent remains balanced.
common_obstacles.solution: Isolate the finishing direction and upper-body connection from a pre-established ankle grip.

common_obstacles.obstacle: The level change breaks your own posture.
common_obstacles.solution: Reduce the reach and rehearse the entry with a coach at a cooperative pace.

common_obstacles.obstacle: A standing setup is copied unchanged from seated guard.
common_obstacles.solution: Review the different starting position and preserve the relevant grip while rebuilding the entry.

common_obstacles.obstacle: Every feint is followed by an attack even when no step occurs.
common_obstacles.solution: Require the selected movement cue before attempting ankle contact.

training_methodology.drilling_approach: BJJGraph practice suggestion: Choose one upper-body grip and identify whether the same-side or opposite ankle is the intended target before lowering your level. Then connect it to standing setup. Compare the first lost control point after each round. Keep the first repetitions cooperative and agree on resistance, space, and reset conditions. Once the starting task is clear, add one defensive option at a time and compare the result with the intended control objective.

flashcards.question: Why is reaching the ankle insufficient to complete an ankle pick?
flashcards.answer: The opponent may remain balanced unless the upper-body connection and finishing direction also support the takedown.

flashcards.question: How should you choose the target ankle?
flashcards.answer: Relate the intended same-side or cross-body target to the upper-body grip and the movement you are trying to create.

flashcards.question: What should a standing setup produce before the attack?
flashcards.answer: It should prompt an observable step or balance change that makes the selected ankle available.

flashcards.question: What changes when studying an ankle pick from seated guard?
flashcards.answer: The starting height and movement differ, so preserve the relevant grip and rebuild the entry instead of copying standing footwork.

flashcards.question: How can you isolate a weak ankle-pick finish?
flashcards.answer: Begin with ankle contact already established and work on the agreed direction against one controlled balance reaction.

flashcards.question: What should you do if a feint produces no useful step?
flashcards.answer: Maintain or rebuild the connection instead of automatically reaching for an ankle that has not become available.
